newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-U.S. Navy surrenders its last strike aircraft.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S. Navy surrenders its last strike aircraft.

text.p: The deck crew call it "Jurassic Park", the corner of the flight deck where they keep the dinosaurs.
The dinosaurs are A-6 Intruders, awkward-looking aircraft that are the only warplanes in the U.S. Navy designed specifically to strike ground targets.
And they are about to become extinct.
The last Intruders are due to be decommissioned in February, leaving the U.S Navy to fill the Intruder's role with fighters merely adapted for ground attack.

"The Intruder has what other carrier aircraft don't have - a heavy payload combined with long range and an ability to attack the target in all weather at very low altitude," said Lieutenant Commander Bob Papadakis, an Intruder bombardier/navigator, as the carrier USS Carl Vinson sailed off the coast of Tasmania.
But the old Intruder is also expensive to maintain.
A squadron of 12 requires 250 maintenance personnel, compared with just 150 for a similar number of F/A-18 Hornets, and with the end of the Cold war the U.S. Navy cannot justify the expense.
The Vinson, visiting Tasmania on its way home from Gulf deployment, is scheduled to send the last of the trusty Intruders off to retirement when it reaches the U.S. West Coast.
No direct replacement is in sight.
When the Intruders are gone, they will be replaced by additional Hornets, adapted fighters that have nothing like the attack capability wielded for three decades by the made-to-measure Intruder.
The 36-year-old Intruder still has the edge over newer aircraft in attacking surface targets. Other planes may be more versatile, but the Intruder is the master of the strike.
It is not, however, a pretty aircraft -- the forward fuselage, with a big bulging canopy, is unusually fat, while the tail is incongruously skinny.
The Intruder is a warplane only its designer could love. Or an enthusiast such as Papadakis, who has flown Intruders for 13 years.
"It may be ugly," he said, perhaps a little hurt at the suggestion. "But that's because the nose is built around the big terrain-clearance radar."
The radar, tailored to ground attacks rather than mid-air dogfights, is another asset the U.S. Navy will lose.

In the 1980s the U.S. Navy planned to replace the Intruder with the A-12 Avenger, a specially-designed strike aircraft that would have been like a scaled-down equivalent of the air force's B-2 stealth bomber.
But then Secretary of Defense Dick Cheney cancelled the super-expensive A-12 in early 1991 even as Allied forces were building up in the Gulf.

Later, with the Soviet threat gone, even the cheaper A-X programme was folded into the current Joint Strike Fighter project, a relatively small aircraft that will be built jointly by the U.S. Air Force, Marines and Britain's Royal Navy to save costs.
Plans in the late 1980s to update the Intruder with new engines, electronics and wings were scaled back. In the end, the existing Intruder fleet got only a modest upgrade.
But when the Intruder entered service in the early 1960s, it had an unprecedented technological advantage.
Developed in the late 1950s, the Intruder was one of the first designs to recognise there was no future in flying higher and faster, as earlier strike aircraft had always sought to do.
Radar, fast-climbing fighters and faster-climbing anti-aircraft missiles meant high-altitude missions over enemy territory had become risky to pilots.
This forced older aircraft such as the B-52 down to lower altitudes, where they were buffeted as they plowed through the thicker, more turbulent air.
"But we learned in the Korean conflict that there was a way to sneak in at low altitude -- and this plane was designed from the beginning to do that," Papadakis said.

The aircraft maker Grumman (now Northrop Grumman) designed the Intruder to take off from aircraft carriers for low-altitude missions. But unlike its contemporaries, the Intruder carried the electronics needed to find and attack targets completely obscured by weather or darkness.

This capability gives the Intruder its ungainly appearance. The fat nose accommodates a large radar that identifies invisible targets while keeping the aircraft from crashing as it skims close to the ground.
The Intruder remained in production for 32 years -- a record almost unrivalled among combat aircraft -- with the last coming off the production line in 1992.
But economics has forced the U.S. Navy to cut back on the number of different types of aircraft it operates, specially expensive planes like the Intruder.
In the Intruder's final mission, the last two squadrons -- Papadakis's and one from the USS Enterprise -- will be decommissioned on February 28 and flown to the Arizona desert for storage.
